episodes.191206: Moisture from the remnants of Atlantic Tropical Storm Alberto surged north up the Gulf of California and into the Mojave Desert, fueling isolated thunderstorms. One storm produced high winds.
episodes.191207: During the afternoon hours a complex of thunderstorms crossed into Indiana from Illinois. A widespread swath of 65 to 75 mph winds occurred from central Terre Haute as far south as Sullivan, with the southeastward path then continuing into Clay, Owen, Greene, and Brown Counties before gradually beginning to weaken as it entered Lawrence and Jackson Counties.||The southern side of Terre Haute saw numerous large trees and power poles snapped or uprooted with widespread property damage to cars and homes along with thousands of power outages.  Clay City and Jasonville also were areas of more concentrated damage with additional trees downed.  The Bloomington ASOS measured 78 mph, which lined up with the town of Bloomington seeing the most significant damage from this event with a large swath of the town seeing widespread tree, power pole, and property damage. ||Spotters later measured a 75 mph wind gust in far southern Brown county where additional tree damage was found but after this point the storm complex gradually weakened with the last damage noted in the Seymour area as the complex moved into an air mass that was more stable following weaker thunderstorms that had occurred earlier in the afternoon.  The storm complex exited south central Indiana around 4:45 PM for a total event time of 2 hours between Terre Haute and Seymour.
episodes.191213: A waterspout was spotted just offshore of Cape San Blas.
episodes.191453: Severe thunderstorms with damaging winds moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon of June 25th with additional storms later in the night into early on the morning of June 26th.
episodes.191594: Severe thunderstorms developed amid an active upper air pattern. Numerous reports of thunderstorm wind gusts were received over Indiana, but at least once instance thunderstorm wind damage was received in northwest Ohio.
episodes.191686: Several rounds of thunderstorms produced strong winds and hail over the Lake Michigan waters during the late evening hours on Monday (6/24) and the early morning hours on Tuesday (6/25).
episodes.191687: Already high river levels, and additional heavy rainfall the evening of June 22nd, led to more river flooding late in June into July over portions of southern WI.
episodes.191688: Isolated thunderstorms developed ahead of a warm front during the late evening on Monday (6/24) producing large hail.  A Quasi-Linear Convective System developed across northwest Wisconsin and tracked southeast through northeastern Wisconsin during the overnight hours into early Tuesday morning (6/25).  The storms produced widespread straight-line wind damage, an isolated tornado, and some flash flooding across the region.
episodes.191704: A small cluster of strong thunderstorms formed along the dryline in far southwest Nebraska moved east through dinner hour into Furnas and Gosper counties. However, the storms did manage to produce pockets of strong winds, including a 63 mph wind gusts at the Cambridge Airport. Tree damage was reported in Gosper county. Though some rain did fall, the combination of the wind and dry ground resulted in blowing dust reported to have dropped the visibility down to one-quarter mile at times.
episodes.191731: A stalled front combined with very hot temperatures led to the development of a few strong thunderstorms across the adjacent maritime waters.
episodes.191853: In the early afternoon of June 25th, a cold front moved into the forecast area from the north, bringing with it a broken QLCS. Two thunderstorms within the QLCS produced severe hail and wind damage in Brown County. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
episodes.191854: In the late afternoon of June 25th, semi-discrete convection ahead of a cold front produced widespread wind damage in central and northeast Missouri. Unfortunately, this resulted in one fatality in Audrain County.
episodes.191894: A multi-day significant heavy rainfall event from June 20-22 resulted in widespread rain totals between 5 and 10 inches with pockets in excess of 15 inches across portions of southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota. As rainfall reached area streams and rivers, major to record flooding was observed, devastating several towns and communities. Extensive overland flooding also resulted in significant impacts and damages. All river crest information is preliminary until made official by the gauge owner.||A Presidential Disaster Declaration was signed for Aurora, Bon Homme, Brule, Charles Mix, Clay, Davison, Douglas, Gregory, Hanson, Hutchinson, Lake, Lincoln, McCook, Miner, Minnehaha, Moody, Sanborn, Turner, Union, and Yankton Counties.
episodes.191897: A multi-day significant heavy rainfall event from June 20-22 resulted in widespread rain totals between 5 and 10 inches with pockets in excess of 15 inches across parts of southeast South Dakota and northwest Iowa. As rainfall reached area streams and rivers and moved downstream, significant flooding was observed along parts of the Missouri River. All river crest information is preliminary until made official by the gauge owner.
episodes.191899: A multi-day significant heavy rainfall event from June 20-22 resulted in widespread rain totals between 5 and 10 inches across portions of southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota. As rainfall reached area streams and rivers, major to record flooding was observed, devastating several towns and communities. Extensive overland flooding also resulted in significant impacts and damages. All river crest information is preliminary until made official by the gauge owner.||A Presidential Disaster Declaration was signed for Buena Vista, Cherokee, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Plymouth, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux, and Woodbury Counties.
episodes.192102: A cold front stalled over the region with an area of low-pressure riding along it, becoming a focal point for shower and thunderstorm development. The steering winds were under 5 miles per hour, allowing storms to stall. This resulted in localized flash flooding in Chesterville and China Maine with road washouts in each community.
episodes.192372: A large complex of thunderstorms tracked across Wisconsin and Michigan during the pre-dawn hours of June 25th...triggering an additional cluster of storms further southwest in the Chicago metropolitan area.  As these storms dropped southeastward, one of the cells grazed Vermilion County...dropping quarter-sized hail near Hoopeston shortly after sunrise.  By mid-morning, a line of thunderstorms had developed along the outflow boundary left behind by the Wisconsin-Michigan complex from central Iowa eastward to southern Lake Michigan.  As the line sagged southward, it produced damaging wind gusts of around 60 mph and sporadic hail as large as quarters as far south as the I-72 corridor.  One of the cells along the line became particularly intense by early afternoon and produced significant crop damage east and southeast of Paris in Edgar County due to wind-driven large hail.  The largest stones were golf ball-sized just north of Dennison.  A wake low generated by the cell produced 60-70 mph wind gusts and additional wind damage across portions of Champaign and Piatt counties after the storm had passed.
episodes.192496: Strong thunderstorm activity developed across the higher terrain areas and foothills to the north and east of Phoenix during the afternoon and early evening hours. A storm complex that developed across the higher terrain areas to the northeast of Phoenix sent a surging outflow boundary westward into the Phoenix metro area with gusty winds in excess of 40 mph as well as areas of blowing dust observed. The gusty winds were enough to cause some minor tree and property damage.
episodes.192524: A couple of discrete severe storms impacted the central to southern Texas Panhandle on the evening of the 25th producing damaging winds and one instance of 1��� hail.  On the 26th, some more discrete severe storms, this time embedded in some widespread thunderstorm activity across the western combined Panhandles produced damaging winds with one instance of hail up to 1��� in diameter. Then on the 27th a line of storms moved in from southeastern Colorado produced hail up to 1��� in diameter in Texas County in the OK Panhandle and a wind gust up to 64 mph in Lipscomb County the far northeastern TX Panhandle.
episodes.192605: An upper trough across the central CONUS instigated numerous clusters of convection across the Southern Plains. One of these clusters contained supercell storm structures as it moved from Kay and Noble Counties into portions of central Oklahoma during the evening of the 25th. Large to very large hail and significant damaging wind gusts were observed along the path of this storm cluster, including across northern/central portions of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area.
episodes.192614: A cluster of strong to severe storms moved across Chicagoland during the night of the 24th immediately followed by a line of storms which went on to impact northern Illinois through the morning of the 25th. The storms produced mostly wind damage, mainly to trees, as well as some marginally severe hail. The storms also resulted in one man being struck by lightning in Marengo.
episodes.192626: A strong thunderstorm moved over northwest Indiana late during the night of the 24th resulting in one report of tree damage in which a tree snapped and fell onto a car near Fowler.
episodes.192627: A line of strong to severe storms pushed south across southern Lake Michigan during the early morning of the 25th.
episodes.192669: Severe storms brought widespread damaging wind gusts and an isolated report of large hail.
episodes.192749: Numerous slow-moving storms occurred on the afternoon of June 25, lasting into the evening. These storms quickly became strong to severe, with multiple becoming supercells, which ended up producing locally heavy rainfall, damaging winds, large hail, and four tornadoes that were generally weak, but still capable of damage. Winds were generally 60 mph or greater with the stronger storms, with a corridor of winds greater than 65 mph. These thunderstorms remained nearly stationary in areas, resulting in nearly 2 to 4 inches of quick rainfall and flash flooding.
episodes.192750: Numerous slow-moving storms occurred on the afternoon of June 25, lasting into the evening. These storms quickly became strong to severe, with multiple becoming supercells, which ended up producing locally heavy rainfall, damaging winds, large hail, and four tornadoes that were generally weak, but still capable of damage. Winds were generally 60 mph or greater with the stronger storms, with a corridor of winds greater than 65 mph. These thunderstorms remained nearly stationary in areas, resulting in nearly 2 to 4 inches of quick rainfall and flash flooding.
episodes.192751: Numerous slow-moving storms occurred on the afternoon of June 25, lasting into the evening. These storms quickly became strong to severe, with multiple becoming supercells, which ended up producing locally heavy rainfall, damaging winds, large hail, and four tornadoes that were generally weak, but still capable of damage. Winds were generally 60 mph or greater with the stronger storms, with a corridor of winds greater than 65 mph. These thunderstorms remained nearly stationary in areas, resulting in nearly 2 to 4 inches of quick rainfall and flash flooding.
episodes.192809: Some isolated severe storms moved across the international border on June 24th. More severe affected northern Minnesota in the afternoon. Most reports were hail, with some funnel clouds.
episodes.192825: Scattered convection occurred throughout the day across the area as a weak cold front dropped slowly south across the area. By afternoon the front had largely stalled near the I-80 corridor and more vigorous convection developed along the front, fed by high instability exceeding 3000 J/kg and steep mid level lapse rates of 7 to 8 C/km. Storms first began near Newton and then back built towards the west along the boundary through the evening. Storms produced large hail and stretching resulted in a huge number of funnel clouds, including pictures with a least visible at the same time. Later in the evening a wave across Nebraska moved into Iowa, sweeping east along the instability gradient that the earlier evening convection developed on. A few damaging wind gusts occurred with this line of storms, however it remained sub severe most of the night.
episodes.192887: A severe thunderstorm developed over the central Black Hills, producing large hail in the Mount Rushmore, Keystone, and Rockerville areas.
episodes.192888: A severe thunderstorm developed quickly over the Silver City area and tracked northeast over the Summerset area, then east-northeast across the southern Meade County plains. Very large hail to over baseball size fell in the Summerset area, causing considerable property damage. Hail diminished some with the storm across the Meade County plains, but winds increased to near 60 mph, before the storm dissipated.
episodes.192890: A large thunderstorm became severe as it moved across portions of the west central South Dakota plains, producing hail and wind gusts to around 60 mph.
episodes.192891: A thunderstorm quickly became severe over northern Meade County, producing large hail from the Mud Butte to Fairpoint areas.
episodes.192892: A supercell thunderstorm developed in the Union Center area and tracked southeast into northeast Pennington County. The storm produced large hail and wind gusts over 60 mph.
episodes.192893: A thunderstorm briefly became severe across portions of southwest Meade County, producing wind gusts to 60 mph in the Hereford area.
episodes.192894: A supercell thunderstorm developed just west of Rapid City, clipping western and southern portions of Rapid City, then tracked onto the plains before weakening over southeast Pennington County. The storm produced hail to over quarter size.
episodes.192896: A large supercell thunderstorm developed over western Jackson County and tracked southeast through Bennett County and into Nebraska. The storm caused considerable damage in Potato Creek and the Martin area with very large hail and strong wind gusts.
episodes.192911: Sea breeze storms produced locally strong wind gusts over a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.192949: On June 25, multiple lines of storms moved across Illinois and into southern Indiana as they followed a northwest to northeast frontal boundary to the southwest. Most of the winds with these lines were sub-severe, but a one tree did fall in Clark County.
episodes.192953: On June 25 and 26, multiple lines of storms moved across Illinois and southern Indiana before entering central Kentucky as they followed a northwest to northeast frontal boundary to the southwest. Most of the winds with these lines were sub-severe, but a few trees and power lines were brought down. One gas station in Jefferson County had the canopy over its gas pumps blow down.
episodes.192995: A warm front moved through the region, forcing isolated storms out in front of it.
episodes.192996: A warm front moved through the region, forcing isolated storms out in front of it.
episodes.193004: A typical summertime pattern fueled numerous showers and thunderstorms over the southeastern Florida metro with diurnal heating and deep moisture pooled over the area on June 25th. Weak low-level winds, out of the west-southwest, brought convective activity to the east coast in the afternoon. Precipitable water values were high, approaching 2 inches. High rainfall values, over much of the east coast, brought the threat for localized flash flooding.
episodes.193128: A strong MCS developed NW of Kentucky and dove southward during the day on June 25. By the time it reached Kentucky in the late afternoon and evening, it lost considerable strength and was falling apart. However, the far eastern fringes remained decently strong, resulting in a few downed trees in Montgomery and Powell Counties.
episodes.193195: Monsoon moisture brought thunderstorms to northern Arizona with a few strong storms.
episodes.193211: Isolated thunderstorms developed over Sheridan County during the early evening hours of June 24th. As this activity tracked east into northern Cherry County, it became severe with strong winds. Winds were estimated at 60 MPH south of Eli in Cherry county.
episodes.193216: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed along a boundary, draped across the central Sandhills during the late afternoon hours of June 25th. This activity became severe with golf ball sized hail. Later that evening, super cell thunderstorms in southern South Dakota, tracked south into western Cherry county. These severe storms produced 4 inch hail in western Cherry county. As the storm tracked into Grant county, it produced a long track, strong tornado, which tracked from near Whitman, to west of Tryon.
episodes.193280: A strong low level jet produced gusty winds over southern Lake Michigan on the morning of the 25th, including one 51 kt gust recorded at the Harrsion-Dever Crib.
episodes.193282: A cluster of mostly sub-severe storms moved across far northern Illinois during the evening of the 25th producing isolated instances of severe hail near Woodstock.
episodes.193311: Heavy rain fell over portions of northern Iowa, especially northwestern Iowa and bordering states later on June 20 through early on June 21. This rainfall caused flash flooding in portions of northwest Iowa and also aided in saturating the soil. As another round of heavy rain fell later on June 21 into the night and morning of June 22, this rainfall led to renewed flash flooding. This rainfall made its way into streams and rivers resulting in significant and record river flooding in northwest Iowa including the West Fork of the Des Moines River. Flooding resulted in massive sandbagging efforts, prolonged road closures and damages, and impacts to home and businesses.||Note: damage estimates are taken from Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management Department and represent total flood damages for the entire county for the month of June. Damages are estimated to have surpassed $12 million in June.
episodes.193344: On June 24th, a lone thunderstorm crossed the Mississippi River into Vernon and Richland counties and produced quarter sized hail as it moved southeast.
episodes.193345: Just after midnight on June 25th, an organized complex of severe storms moved through Taylor and northern Clark counties producing tree damage in the city of Medford.
episodes.193361: Above normal rainfall over the course of June, combined with a robust rainfall event between June 20th and 22nd, led to widespread river flooding across portions of southeast Minnesota. Rainfall amounts upwards of 7 inches between the 20th and 22nd allowed the Mississippi River, Cedar River and many other river basins in southeast Minnesota to enter flood stage towards the end of June. Flooding along the Mississippi River mainstem continued into July.
episodes.193392: A supercell thunderstorm developed over Jackson County and tracked southeast into south central South Dakota. The storm produced some large hail and wind gusts to over 70 mph.
episodes.193435: Strong heating and deep moisture near a weak surface trough led to thunderstorms capable of producing small hail and damaging winds.
episodes.193445: A cluster of slow moving thunderstorms along a warm front produced heavy rain and one severe hail report over south central WI.
episodes.193447: Numerous thunderstorms along a warm front brought large hail, damaging winds, and some flooding to eastern WI. Later in the day, scattered thunderstorms along the cold front brought large hail to the Janesville area.
episodes.193525: An anomalously moist environment was conducive to drenching thunderstorms. This resulted in two instances of urban flooding from 1 to 2 inches of rainfall.
episodes.193527: Instances of downed trees and power lines were reported, along with some hail, as thunderstorms moved through the state. Heavy rainfall was also reported, primarily in Michigan.
episodes.193545: A wake low from a decaying thunderstorm complex generated high winds at Rock of Ages Light during the morning of the 25th.
episodes.193547: A wake low from a decaying thunderstorm complex caused very strong wind gusts over portions of the northern Bay of damage over south central Upper Michigan on the morning of the 25th.
episodes.193564: Thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a warm front across northwest Wisconsin during the evening hours of the 24th. Storms quickly became severe in a very unstable and highly sheared environment as the grew upscale into a large complex during the late evening and early overnight hours. Damaging wind gusts comprised the majority of reports with numerous trees downed and buildings damaged along with a measured wind gust of 71 mph. A few hail and flash flooding reports were received as well.
episodes.193619: Multiple funnel clouds were observed and reported on June 25th in the Corpus Christi area when conditions were ideal for tropical funnel clouds: light winds through the low-levels, significant moisture, and weak convergence with the seabreeze. No injuries or damage was observed.
episodes.193743: An isolated waterspout was observed in Florida Bay waters northeast of Marathon as result of a reverse convective cloud line.
episodes.193862: Lingering moisture after a monsoonal/post-tropical moisture surge combined with some enhanced instability and lift from a passing shortwave to produce scattered to widespread convection across eastern Utah and western Colorado. Drying surface levels allowed for some enhancement of outflow winds from showers and storms as falling precipitation evaporated before reaching the ground.
episodes.193866: Despite high pressure building into the region, enough residual moisture from a monsoonal push earlier in the week remained to spawn afternoon convection over eastern Utah and western Colorado. Multiple weak waves added some extra lift and instability, while drying surface levels helped to enhance outflow winds.
episodes.193922: A series of shortwave troughs traversing the northern CONUS brought unsettled weather to the area for the end of June. On the 21st, a stationary front was draped across northeast Nebraska into Iowa. Ahead of one of the aforementioned shortwave troughs, several rounds of strong thunderstorms developed near this frontal zone and moved across northeast Nebraska. At 8 pm on the 21st, radar imagery showed training thunderstorms had set up across central Nebraska. These storms moved into east-central Nebraska dropping 2 to 6 inches of rain across the Platte River Basin. As a result, minor flooding was observed along the Platte River in Dodge, Saunders, Douglas and Sarpy Counties. Further north in Knox County, additional rounds of thunderstorms brought flooding to the Ponca Creek, prompting emergency management to deploy sand bags. Flooding in these locations continued for several days before subsiding the 23rd.||Behind this first shortwave, a shortwave ridge moved out into the central Plains accompanied by a surface high pressure system. Afternoon high temperatures in the 90s and dew points in the mid and upper 70s brought excessive heat to much of eastern Nebraska and western Iowa the afternoons of the 24th and the 25th. Excessive heat was most widespread on the 24th, with heat indices across the entire WFO ranging from 107 to 120 degrees. Afternoon thunderstorms on the 25th mitigated excessive heat, though heat indices did hit 110 in far southwest Iowa.||On the 25th, another shortwave trough brought more unsettled weather to the region. A surface front was draped across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa when the first convection initiated over downtown Omaha. This storm quickly became intense, producing multiple instances of 3 to 4 inch hail in the Omaha metro. As this storm weakened over eastern Sarpy County, additional strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northeast Nebraska. While the most widespread hazard was large hail up to the size of golf balls, two tornadoes were confirmed in Madison County. Later that evening, a bow echo developed and moved through the northern Omaha Metro, bringing wind gusts up to 90 miles per hour at Eppley Airfield and into northern Pottawattamie County. An additional line of storms developed after dark that night across southeast Nebraska and produced scattered damaging wind gusts, the highest of which was an 83 mph wind gust measured by emergency management in Jefferson County.||The unsettled weather at the end of June brought widespread excessive rain to much of southeast South Dakota and Northwest Iowa. Rainfall estimated from these storms showed a swath of 4 to 8 inches of rain that fell between Sioux Falls and Sioux City. The result of this rain and additional rain across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa was river flooding along the Missouri and Little Sioux the last week of June and into July. Flooding during this time frame resulted in numerous road closures, including I-29 between Council Bluffs and Missouri Valley. This stretch of the interstate was closed beginning midnight the night of the 25th, and remained closed through the end of the month. Levee breaches in Monona County on the 25th prompted several evacuations, as resultant flash flooding inundated multiple county roads and homesteads. No injuries or fatalities were reported from this. While flooding subsided in and north of the Omaha metro by the end of the month, river flooding along the Missouri persisted into the first week of July.

While many of the 19 counties reporting these cases masked the exact number of hospitalizations in order to protect personal health information, it was released that there were 37 heat related hospitalizations in Douglas County, 13 in Lancaster County, and 7 in Sarpy County. The vast majority of these heat related illnesses (66.25%) occurred at work or while participating in outdoor recreation. 12.5% were among the homeless population, and 8.75% of heat related hospitalizations were due to a lack of air conditioning. episodes.194012: Storms developed in south central Kansas and increased in coverage across southeast Kansas during the evening hours. These storms produced large hail ranging from quarter to baseball size. Another round of storms developed late in the overnight into the early morning hours of the 26th. These storms produced dominantly damaging wind gusts ranging from 58 to 70 mph in southeast Kansas. There was some tree and roof damage reported n Chanute and Iola.
episodes.194136: Numerous thunderstorms along a warm front brought strong to severe winds across east central WI nearshores and open water zones.
episodes.194325: The Lake Erie region resided in the warm and humid sector during the morning of the 25th through early evening of the 26th as a cold front drifted southeastward from the Upper Midwest to southern ON, southeastern Lower MI, and northern IN. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell showers and thunderstorms moved southeastward across the western-half of Lake Erie on the 25th, weakened as the convection outpaced greater instability and encountered a tight westerly gradient in weak to moderate MUCAPE, and was followed by a potent wake low accompanied by a tight MSLP gradient. The line of showers and thunderstorms, and the trailing wake low generated gale-force convective wind gusts along and near the northwest OH lakeshore amidst moderate DCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively. ||On the 26th, additional scattered to numerous multicell showers and thunderstorms developed over Lake Erie, ahead of the front, and persisted generally eastward while encountering weak to moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, respectively, and moderate to strong effective bulk shear in the warm and moist sector. These storms produced additional gale-force convective wind gusts along the northern OH shore.
episodes.194451: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of June 25th, storms brought widespread severe wind gusts as well as some hail to a large portion of Missouri.

The river then fell below flood stage on the morning of June 27th. For a more comprehensive description of flood damage, please see other entries for Dakota County.

The river then fell below flood stage on the morning of June 27th. For a more comprehensive description of flood damage, please see other entries for Union County.

The Missouri River at Sioux City rose above flood stage the evening of June 24th, cresting around 2.23 feet above flood stage (32.23 feet) on June 25th. The river then fell below flood stage on the morning of June 27th. For a more comprehensive description of flood damage, please see other entries for Woodbury County.
Heavy rain from slow moving thunderstorms caused flooding over ME-32 in Windsor resulting in the road closure.

A thunderstorm moving over the city of Montrose late in the afternoon of the 24th produced strong to severe wind gusts, including one gust to 70 mph. This gust was recorded at the KMTJ ASOS at Montrose Regional Airport at 6:50 PM MDT. Damage was associated with this storm, with reports of several large tree limbs blown down.
Thunderstorm wind gusts, estimated at 60 MPH, were reported at this location along with pea sized hail.
Emergency Manager relays 2 inch hail at Red Lake report.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri. The Missouri River flooding in Nemaha County did not crest until July 1, and will be included on in July StormData. At 8:30 am CDT on 6/26, emergency management sent in photos of flooding at the Brownville Campground.
A lot of quarter size hail, with a few near golf ball size.
Hail to over baseball size fell for 20 minutes.

Alachua County SO reports a road closure of SR-121, locally NW 34th Street, near NW 5th Avenue in Gainesville due to a large tree being blown down from the thunderstorm and blocking the roadway. No injuries were reported. Time was estimated by radar. The cost of damage was unknown, but it was estimated for inclusion of the event in Storm Data.

Tents became airborne and large limbs fell from a tree in the center median of 107th Ave intersecting with Happy Valley Road in Surprise. Wind gusts were estimated at between 40-50 mph based on nearby observing sites. No injuries were reported.
Golf ball to tennis ball size hail.

The river then fell below flood stage on the evening of June 26th. For a more comprehensive description of flood damage, please see other entries for Sanborn County.
A photo was received showing the top two-thirds of a tree that had been snapped off.
All lanes of US 63 were covered with 6 to 10 inches of rushing water in Hayward. There were some localized areas where water was up to 2 feet deep.
Penny size hail fell in Lac Du Flambeau. The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

An EF1 tornado developed about 2 miles northeast of Spragueville in Jackson County Iowa Tuesday evening. The tornado damaged a barn and trees at a farmstead, then continued south/southwest before hitting another farmstead. The tornado caused significant damage to a large outbuilding, then lifted in crop land. Maximum winds were estimated around 100 mph, and the path width was an estimated 50 yards. The tornado path length was nearly one mile. This was likely a landspout, or non-supercell tornado.

One direct fatality occurred 5 miles north of Martinsburg when an old, dilapidated barn on Highway 54 collapsed on an individual seeking shelter from the thunderstorm. Large trees and tree limbs were blown down in Vandalia, Laddonia, and Mexico. Siding was also blown off a church south of Mexico Airport (MYJ), power poles were knocked down by tree limbs in Vandalia, and a roof was blown off a trailer in Laddonia. Other communities in the storm's path are Scott's Corner, Rush Hill, and Martinsburg.

This storm began producing severe hail in a swath from Council Bluffs to eastern Sarpy County. A non-supercell, or landspout tornado touched down in a field about 2 miles north of Ely in Linn County Iowa Tuesday evening. The tornado caused crop damage and moved very slowly to the southeast. The tornado then snapped large tree limbs along Ivanhoe Road, and damaged a power pole cross member. The tornado also lifted some loose asphalt and tossed it a short distance away. The tornado then moved through a grove of trees before lifting in a field. The tornado was rated EF0, with maximum winds estimated around 85 mph. The path width was estimated around 50 yards and the tornado was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes.
